scenes.visual: Title card 'Downhill in Pressure' over a faint branching vessel tree drawn left to right. COLOUR MAP (both films): pressure and the hydrostatic push ORANGE; oncotic pull BLUE; red cells RED dots; resistance PURPLE bars; total cross-section TEAL bars; lymph GREEN; vessel walls charcoal outlines. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Blood moves fastest in your widest artery and slowest in your narrowest vessels. How can narrower mean slower? A single river channel does the opposite. Where its cross-section shrinks, the same water has to speed up.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a wide charcoal tube labelled 'aorta' with RED dots streaming quickly. Right: a hair-thin tube labelled 'capillary' with RED dots creeping. A small inset of one river channel narrows and its blue flow lines speed up, stamped 'one channel, same water: smaller cross-section = faster'. A question mark appears between the two vessels.
scenes.narration: Blood moves fastest in your widest artery and slowest in your narrowest vessels. How can narrower mean slower? A single river channel does the opposite. Where its cross-section shrinks, the same water has to speed up.

scenes.tts: Start with what makes blood flow along a vessel. In a level tube, fluid flows only from higher pressure to lower pressure. Equal pressure at both ends drives no flow, however high that pressure is.
scenes.visual: One horizontal tube between two ORANGE pressure columns, small label 'level tube, no pump inside'. Left column rises above right: RED dots flow left to right. Then both columns rise to the same tall height, labelled 'equal pressure': the dots stop dead, label 'no difference, no flow'.
scenes.narration: Start with what makes blood flow along a vessel. In a level tube, fluid flows only from higher pressure to lower pressure. Equal pressure at both ends drives no flow, however high that pressure is.

scenes.tts: How much flows depends on two things. One is the pressure difference between the ends. The other is the resistance in the way. Flow equals the pressure difference divided by the resistance.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE gap between the columns is bracketed 'P in minus P out'. A PURPLE block labelled 'R' slides into the tube and the dots slow. The rule types on screen: 'Q = (P_in − P_out) / R', with Q labelled 'flow'. It stays pinned at the top corner for the rest of the film.
scenes.narration: How much flows depends on two things. One is the pressure difference between the ends. The other is the resistance in the way. Flow equals the pressure difference divided by the resistance.

scenes.tts: Now lay out the whole circulation as one branching tree. The aorta splits into arteries, then arterioles, then capillaries. The capillaries gather again into veins that return to the heart.
scenes.visual: A schematic tree grows left to right: one thick aorta, a few arteries, many arterioles, a dense fan of capillaries, then merging veins on the right ending at a heart icon. Each level labelled under it. Label 'schematic, not to scale'.
scenes.narration: Now lay out the whole circulation as one branching tree. The aorta splits into arteries, then arterioles, then capillaries. The capillaries gather again into veins that return to the heart.

scenes.tts: Above the tree, follow the pressure. It falls all the way from the aorta to the heart's right atrium. It falls most steeply across the arterioles.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE pressure line draws itself above the tree, starting at '93 mmHg' over the aorta and ending at '3 mmHg' over the veins, both as on-screen text. The line is gently sloped over arteries, plunges steeply over the arterioles, then flattens. A bracket over the plunge: 'steepest drop'. Shape labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Above the tree, follow the pressure. It falls all the way from the aorta to the heart's right atrium. It falls most steeply across the arterioles.

scenes.tts: Arterioles have walls of smooth muscle. When the muscle tightens, the arteriole narrows. In an ideal tube, resistance rises with the fourth power of a falling radius. A small squeeze makes a large change.
scenes.visual: Zoom on one arteriole: a charcoal tube wrapped in a muscle cuff. The cuff tightens and the tube narrows slightly; beside it a PURPLE resistance bar shoots up far more than the radius changed. On screen: 'R ∝ 1 / r^4 (ideal tube)'. No numbers.
scenes.narration: Arterioles have walls of smooth muscle. When the muscle tightens, the arteriole narrows. In an ideal tube, resistance rises with the fourth power of a falling radius. A small squeeze makes a large change.

scenes.tts: So arterioles act like taps. Nerves, hormones and local signals set their tone. Tightening one organ's arterioles cuts that organ's share of the blood.
scenes.visual: Back to the tree. Two branches lead to organ icons labelled 'gut' and 'muscle'. The gut branch's arterioles tighten (PURPLE bars rise) and RED dots thin out in that branch; a small share bar beside it shrinks, label 'gut's share falls'. Small tags 'nerves', 'hormones', 'local signals' point at the cuffs.
scenes.narration: So arterioles act like taps. Nerves, hormones and local signals set their tone. Tightening one organ's arterioles cuts that organ's share of the blood.

scenes.tts: But a capillary is narrower than a typical arteriole. On its own, it can resist more. So which level sets most of the resistance?
scenes.visual: One capillary and one arteriole side by side, enlarged; the capillary's PURPLE bar is taller than the arteriole's, small label 'one vessel: length and blood's thickness count too'. Two labelled buttons appear: 'arterioles' and 'capillaries', under a question card.
scenes.narration: But a capillary is narrower than a typical arteriole. On its own, it can resist more. So which level sets most of the resistance?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer counts down at bottom right.

scenes.tts: The arterioles. Most capillaries are not lined up in a chain. They lie side by side, in huge numbers. Side by side, paths share the flow, so together they resist less.
scenes.visual: The single capillary multiplies into a wide fan of parallel capillaries fed by one arteriole, label 'many side by side (schematic; real beds also branch and rejoin)'. RED dots split among them. The fan's combined PURPLE bar shrinks below the arteriole's bar. The 'arterioles' button lights up.
scenes.narration: The arterioles. Most capillaries are not lined up in a chain. They lie side by side, in huge numbers. Side by side, paths share the flow, so together they resist less.

scenes.tts: Now return to speed. In this simplified tree at steady state, no blood bypasses the capillaries. So the same flow crosses every level.
scenes.visual: A RED 'flow counter' gate sits across the aorta and another across the whole capillary fan; both tick at the same rate, on screen '5 L per min' at each gate and a small label 'steady state; simplified tree, no shunts'.
scenes.narration: Now return to speed. In this simplified tree at steady state, no blood bypasses the capillaries. So the same flow crosses every level.

scenes.tts: Speed is that flow divided by the total cross-section at each level. Each capillary is tiny. But together their cross-section far exceeds the aorta's.
scenes.visual: Under the tree, TEAL bars of total cross-section rise for each level: short under the aorta ('about 4 cm²'), taller under the arterioles, towering under the capillaries ('about 3,000 cm²'), shrinking again under the veins. On screen: 'velocity = flow / total area'.
scenes.narration: Speed is that flow divided by the total cross-section at each level. Each capillary is tiny. But together their cross-section far exceeds the aorta's.

scenes.tts: Spread the same flow over that huge area, and it has to move slowly. That is why blood creeps through the capillaries, the narrowest vessels of all.
scenes.visual: RED dots race through the aorta (on screen 'about 21 cm/s') and enter the capillary fan, where they slow to a crawl (on screen 'about 0.03 cm/s'). The TEAL capillary bar pulses.
scenes.narration: Spread the same flow over that huge area, and it has to move slowly. That is why blood creeps through the capillaries, the narrowest vessels of all.

scenes.tts: So narrow does not, by itself, mean slow. A single narrow tube carrying the whole flow would speed blood up. What matters is the total area at each level.
scenes.visual: The river inset returns: one narrow channel, dots fast. Then it branches into many channels side by side, total width labelled, and the dots slow. Label 'one narrow tube: faster; many in parallel: slower'.
scenes.narration: So narrow does not, by itself, mean slow. A single narrow tube carrying the whole flow would speed blood up. What matters is the total area at each level.

scenes.tts: That slow passage gives blood time to trade with the tissues. And fluid crossing the capillary wall obeys the same rule: a pressure difference over a resistance.
scenes.visual: Close-up of one capillary, RED dots creeping. Faint ORANGE arrows begin to point outward through the wall, and a few BLUE arrows point inward, unlabelled, as a teaser of the wall. The pinned rule in the corner glows.
scenes.narration: That slow passage gives blood time to trade with the tissues. And fluid crossing the capillary wall obeys the same rule: a pressure difference over a resistance.

scenes.visual: Hex card. Line: 'Flow follows a pressure difference, divided by the resistance.'
